verses.text: In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah, and built Ramah, that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.
Then Asa brought out silver and gold out of the treasures of Yahweh’s house and of the king’s house, and sent to Ben Hadad king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, saying,

“Let there be a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent you silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”
Ben Hadad listened to king Asa, and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel; and they struck Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage cities of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and let his work cease.
Then Asa the king took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Rama, and its timber, with which Baasha had built; and he built Geba and Mizpah with them.

At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said to him, “Because you have relied on the king of Syria, and have not relied on Yahweh your God, therefore the army of the king of Syria has escaped out of your hand.
Weren’t the Ethiopians and the Lubim a huge army, with chariots and horsemen exceeding many? Yet, because you relied on Yahweh, he delivered them into your hand.

For Yahweh’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. You have done foolishly in this; for from now on you will have wars.”
Then Asa was angry with the seer, and put him in the prison; for he was in a rage with him because of this thing. Asa oppressed some of the people at the same time.
Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa was diseased in his feet. His disease was exceedingly great: yet in his disease he didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians.
Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the forty-first year of his reign.

They buried him in his own tomb, which he had dug out for himself in David’s city, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art; and they made a very great fire for him.

footnotes.content: Baasha's fortress at Ramah was meant to cut Asa off—to isolate and squeeze him. How it reminds me of the Lord's faithfulness: even when we feel hemmed in by trouble, He sees the whole country we can't see. Asa had known victory through trust before; I wonder what he'd forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa raided Yahweh's treasury itself—the sacred storehouse—to pay a foreign king. That detail stings. When we grow anxious, how quickly we spend the very thing meant to remind us we are held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The language is smooth, diplomatic, reasonable: *Let there be a treaty.* Yet Asa is proposing to break Ben Hadad's earlier pledge to Baasha. I see how easy it is to dress up faithlessness in the grammar of strategy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ben Hadad sent his armies and they struck the northern cities—Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim. The kingdoms of Israel splintered. What Asa bought with silver was other people's suffering. The Lord's way rarely buys peace that way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baasha stopped his work. Asa got what he wanted—outward, immediate relief. But notice: he bought it from the outside in, not from the Lord down. The problem was merely postponed, not solved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa dismantled Baasha's fortress and rebuilt Geba and Mizpah as his own defenses. He was making his faith in walls instead of in Yahweh, stone by stone, and calling it victory. The victory would not last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hanani the seer—his name means *gracious*—brings the rebuke that wounds because it's true: Asa relied on the king of Syria instead of Yahweh, and so the Syrian king escaped him in ways that mattered. The Lord doesn't force faithfulness; He makes known what unfaithfulness has cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This verse opens a window back—the Ethiopians and Lubim came with overwhelming numbers and chariots, yet Asa won when he relied on Yahweh then. He knew that road. The seer is asking: why take a different path now?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh's eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth." He searches not for the mighty, but for the whole-hearted—those who turn to Him without dividing their trust. Asa's heart had divided, and the seer saw it clear as glass. The Lord still offers strength to anyone who turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A rebuke stings most when it's accurate. Asa's rage with Hanani and his imprisonment of the seer show a king whose heart had already broken faith—now pride won't let the truth be spoken. I've seen the same: how quickly we can move from faithlessness to cruelty toward whoever names it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The acts of Asa, first and last." History records both the victories and the fall—the young king who trusted God and the aging king who turned to silver and physicians and imprisonment. We are known for the whole story we live, not just the bright chapters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa's feet diseased, his sickness extreme—and he sought physicians, not Yahweh. He'd already taught himself not to trust the Lord when he bought a foreign king's alliance. The pattern doesn't break easily; unfaithfulness was now his habit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa rested with his fathers after forty-one years—a long reign that began in faithfulness and ended in a turn away from the Lord he'd known. Not every story has a repentance within its frame. Some end as they end, and the Lord still holds them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asa buried in David's city, wrapped in spices and honor—readers today hear an echo of how the Lord honors even a king whose faith grew cold, giving him rest in the city of David. Mercy catches us even where our faithlessness reached its depth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
